lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- Who Said What
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 13 -- Who Said What
lesson.grammar_point: reporting verbs with nuance and their patterns

listenings.text: Let me try to sum up, and please stop me if I get any of this wrong. Our first speaker contends that the scheme has worked, and that the cost being quoted by its critics is exaggerated by roughly a third. Our second speaker conceded at the start that waiting times have fallen, which I do not think anybody expected her to concede, and her objection is to the design rather than to the result. And our third speaker claims that the underlying data are unreliable. I have used the word claims deliberately, and I want to say why. He has not produced the alternative figures, and until he does, claims is the honest verb. If he produces them next week, I will use a different one.

The verb we argue about most in this building is claimed. Some people will tell you it is neutral. It is not. Claimed tells the reader, quietly, that you should not believe this person, and once you notice it you cannot stop noticing it. My test is simple and slightly uncomfortable. Would I use the same verb about somebody I agreed with? If the answer is no, I change it. And there is one that slips past everybody, including me, and it is point out. She pointed out that the date was wrong. That does not report a claim, it asserts a fact and attributes it, in three words, and nobody in the room ever objects to it because it sounds like a small polite verb. It is not a small polite verb. It is a verdict.

extra_audio.text: Nora says the difficult part of her job is summarising three speakers in ninety seconds. He observes that any verb she chooses is already a judgement. She agrees, and explains that conceded, acknowledged and agreed produce three different scenes. He asks what she uses when she does not want to take a side. She answers that she uses said, and that even said is not neutral.
